headline: Philosopher Asks: Is Water From Different Cities Actually Different Water?
subheadline: Viral lecture series explores whether location transforms H2O into distinct substances
summary: A philosophy professor's lecture questioning whether 'New York water' and 'Los Angeles water' are fundamentally the same substance has sparked citywide debates about local identity.
content:
When Dr. Patricia Huang asked her Introduction to Philosophy class whether water from New York and water from Los Angeles are 'the same water,' she expected a brief discussion about chemical composition. What she got was a semester-long odyssey that has now spawned a viral lecture series with 847,000 views.

'Chemically, yes, H2O is H2O,' Dr. Huang explained in her now-famous opening lecture. 'But is chemistry the only thing that defines a substance? New York water has traveled through New York pipes, filtered through New York treatment plants, touched New York air. At what point does it become... New York water?'

The question has ignited fierce debate in comment sections across Threadit and Chirper. New York residents have rallied around the city's famously high-quality tap water, with some arguing that the specific mineral content from upstate reservoirs creates a categorically distinct substance.

'There's a reason New York pizza and bagels taste different,' wrote u/BrooklynH2O on Threadit. 'It's the water. Our water is New York water. You can't replicate it. It has absorbed the essence of the city.'

Los Angeles residents countered that their water's journey from the Colorado River gives it its own distinct character. 'Our water has traveled through deserts,' wrote Chirper user @SoCalSips. 'It has known struggle. LA water has perseverance built into its molecular memory.'

Dr. Huang's lecture series explores increasingly complex territory. In episode four, she asks whether water that evaporates from the ocean and falls as rain in Kansas is 'the same water' or whether the journey transformed it. Episode seven examines whether ice and liquid water share an identity or are 'the same substance in different life stages.'

'We assume substances have fixed identities,' Dr. Huang said in a recent interview. 'But everything is in flux. The water in your glass right now was once in a cloud, maybe in the ocean, maybe in a dinosaur. Is it the same water? What makes water water?'

Critics have called the inquiry 'deliberately obtuse.' Dr. James Chen, a colleague at Hartwell University, argued that 'chemical composition is the only scientifically meaningful metric for substance identity. Everything else is poetry.'

Dr. Huang smiled when presented with this critique. 'Chemistry tells us what something is made of. Philosophy asks what something is. Those are different questions. And both are worth asking.'

Her next lecture, titled 'Is Ice Just Water's Nap?', is scheduled for release next week.
author: Melissa Park, Higher Education
